facts.text: Those opening credits fade in and out, scattered across footage of the flowing river.
The bridge crash cost director Herk Harvey just $12. Lecompton, Kansas let him film for free as long as he replaced the damaged railing afterward.
Drive-In Totals: No breasts (1962). Nineteen dead bodies. Approximately 15 zombies. One motor vehicle chase, with watery crash. Zombie bus tour. Church organ Fu. Zombie Fu.
Harvey's crew consisted of only five other people.
Budget: about $30,000. Harvey raised $17,000 in cash by asking Lawrence businessmen to invest $500 each; the other $13,000 was deferred.
Harvey and writer John Clifford both waived their pay to make the film under budget.
Harvey rented the ruined Saltair Pavilion from the Salt Lake City Chamber of Commerce for one week. The price: $50.
Candace Hilligoss was the only professional actor in the film. She turned down a part in Violent Midnight (1963) to take the lead.
Harvey reportedly thought Hilligoss was 'too dowdy' at first and considered recasting her.
No money for rear-projection car shots, so Harvey used a battery-powered hand-held Arriflex to film inside moving cars.
The Man's face in the car window was done with an angled mirror placed on the far side of the glass.
Harvey wanted 'the look of Bergman and the feel of Cocteau.'
The department store scenes were shot guerrilla style. Harvey paid a saleslady $25 to ignore the crew.
The department store is the famous Z.C.M.I. in Salt Lake City.
The organ factory in the film is the real Reuter Organ Company in Lawrence, Kansas.
The organ score is by Kansas City organist Gene Moore. Locations like the Saltair and the church organ pushed the film toward an all-organ soundtrack.
Portions are tinted faint cyan whenever Mary is in an altered mental state. 'Real' scenes stay pure black-and-white.
Sidney Berger, who plays creepy neighbor John, was a drama teacher. His students included Randy Quaid, Dennis Quaid and Brent Spiner.
Roger Ebert called Berger's character the 'definitive study of a nerd in lust.' Berger loved quoting it.
Berger is reportedly blind in the eye used for the keyhole shot.
Drive-In Totals: Drive-In Academy Award nominations for Candace Hilligoss, for 'I don't belong in the world'; Frances Feist, for 'You can take all the baths you want'; Art Ellison, as the minister.
Assistant director Reza Badiyi later designed famous TV openings, including Hawaii Five-O, Get Smart and The Mary Tyler Moore Show.
Harvey and Clifford were Centron employees, an industrial-film company in Lawrence. Interiors were shot at Centron's studio.
One reel was ruined in processing: ghouls slowly rising from behind rotting pylons and walking across the flats. It was overexposed and never made the film.
Harvey played The Man himself. At the 1989 reunion he gave interviews in full ghoul makeup.
The film lacked a copyright notice on its prints, which automatically put it in the public domain in the US.
The ghouls dancing at the pavilion were hired from a University of Utah dance class.
The film shot in three weeks, with the cast and crew working seven days a week.
Drive-In Totals: Sidney Berger, as the letch next door, nominated for 'You're gonna need me in the evening, you just don't know it yet.'
Original release was a box-office failure, on a double bill with The Devil's Messenger. Late-night TV later built its cult following.
Hilligoss's agent refused to represent her any longer after seeing the film.
Drive-In owners trimmed the film from 84 minutes to as little as 75 to squeeze in more showings. Theatrical prints ran about 78.
After the film, Harvey went back to industrial films. His distributor Herts-Lion sent a royalty check that bounced, and the company folded in 1964.
Roger Ebert called it a 'lost episode of The Twilight Zone' with an 'intriguing power.'
George A. Romero cited this film as an inspiration for Night of the Living Dead (1968).
Lana Del Rey sampled Mary's line 'I don't belong in the world' in her song '13 Beaches.'
In 2016 RiffTrax Live riffed the film, and Michael J. Nelson recorded a commentary track for the 2009 Legend Films colorized DVD.
The Criterion Collection released it as spine #63.
The Saltair was damaged by fires in 1967 and 1970. It was rebuilt smaller in the 1980s and is now a small concert venue.
Hilligoss turned down an offer to appear in the 1998 remake. She had written her own sequel treatment in the late 1980s.
Hilligoss was paid about $2,500. She described the job as a 'take-the-money-and-run type of situation.'
Slant Magazine ranked it #32 on its '100 Best Horror Movies of All Time.'
Herk Harvey directed over 400 educational and industrial films at Centron. This was his only feature.
The film inspired Sole Survivor (1984), which is said to have inspired Final Destination (2000).
Harvey later played a farmer in the nuclear TV movie The Day After (1983), mostly filmed in Lawrence.
Drive-In Totals: Herk Harvey nominated for producing, directing, and playing the Head Zombie. Also in the Drive-In Hall of Fame.
Drive-In Totals: Four stars. Joe Bob says check it out.
